content: Individuals who have been in contact with someone diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB) should undergo a thorough evaluation to rule out TB and other diseases that may cause similar symptoms. If active TB disease is excluded following clinical assessment or national guidelines, these individuals, regardless of age, should be offered TB preventive treatment (TPT). For HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older, the absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings can be used to rule out active TB disease before initiating preventive treatment. Testing for latent TB infection (LTBI) can be performed using either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). Recommended options for LTBI treatment, irrespective of HIV status, include: 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, A 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, A 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin, A 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have a positive or unknown LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). This should be provided regardless of whether the individual is on antiretroviral therapy (ART), their degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy status. TB remains the leading infectious cause of death globally. TPT is critical in preserving health, reducing mortality and transmission, and preventing catastrophic costs for families. Governments and donors must take proactive measures to ensure access to TPT for all high-risk populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend prioritizing populations for TPT based on the following criteria: High prevalence of TB infection, High risk of progression to active TB disease, High incidence of TB disease compared to the general population, or A favorable benefit-risk ratio for TPT. Two broad groups are identified for systematic TPT eligibility assessment: 1. Individuals at elevated risk of progression from TB infection to active disease, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV), patients with silicosis, those preparing for or receiving anti-TNF treatment, dialysis, or organ/hematologic transplantation. 2. Individuals with increased likelihood of TB exposure, such as household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases, prisoners, healthcare workers, recent immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. Children under 5 years of age who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases and are found not to have active TB should receive TPT, even if LTBI testing is unavailable. Similarly, children aged 5 years and older, adolescents, and adults in contact with confirmed TB cases may also be offered TPT after ruling out active TB. For household contacts of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) patients, TPT may be considered based on individualized risk assessment and clinical justification. Limited evidence supports specific regimens for MDR-TB contacts, but studies have used levofloxacin with or without ethambutol/ethionamide for six months. TPT should only be initiated after ruling out active TB and conducting a careful risk assessment, including exposure intensity, source disease certainty, and drug resistance patterns. PLHIV are approximately 20 times more likely to develop active TB than those without HIV and should be prioritized for systematic evaluation and TPT in all settings. Despite advancements in ART, TB remains the leading cause of AIDS-related deaths globally. Evidence shows that TPT improves survival in PLHIV, even when they are on ART. TPT also provides additional protection when administered immediately after completing TB treatment in PLHIV. Children living with HIV (CLHIV) aged 12 months or older should be considered for TPT regardless of TB contact history, ART status, or LTBI testing availability. Infants under 12 months living with HIV who have been in contact with a TB patient should also receive TPT if active TB is ruled out. Infants born to HIV-infected mothers are at risk of early TB infection due to maternal exposure, and TPT should be considered for these infants if they show no signs of TB disease. For individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematologic transplantation, or with silicosis, systematic LTBI testing and treatment are recommended. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are not routinely recommended for individuals with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco smoking, or underweight unless they belong to other high-risk groups. However, these populations may still be considered for TPT on a case-by-case basis, especially if they have multiple risk factors for TB or are at heightened risk of unfavorable outcomes. National programs should integrate TPT services with active TB case finding (ACF) among at-risk populations to increase coverage with minimal additional investment. For example, household contacts of HIV-positive TB patients should also be offered HIV counseling and testing. Similarly, malnutrition screening and assessment should be conducted during contact investigations when relevant. Key interventions to minimize TB recurrence include completing the initial TB treatment course, implementing effective infection control measures, and providing secondary TPT.
